prompt: What is the difference between an eligible and an active assignment of Owner, once the eligible one has been activated?
hint: Compare what the role allows, not how it was obtained.

choices.text: None in what it allows
choices.why: Right. What differs is the hours it is held and the record of why.

choices.text: The activated one allows reading but not writing
choices.why: Activation gives the whole role; PIM does not trim it.

choices.text: The activated one cannot create role assignments, as a safety measure
choices.why: An activated Owner is exactly as powerful as a standing one.

choices.text: The active one is limited to one resource group
choices.why: Scope is chosen for each assignment, whatever its type.

prompt: Why does the lesson call removing a role and adding it back by hand "the wrong fix"?
hint: What happens on the day the person who adds roles is away?

choices.text: Because Azure refuses to re-create an assignment that was deleted
choices.why: Nothing stops re-creating it. The problem is people, not Azure.

choices.text: It drifts back to standing access, unrecorded
choices.why: Right. It depends on somebody remembering, and leaves nothing behind.

choices.text: Because deleted assignments stay in the 5,000 limit
choices.why: A deleted assignment no longer counts.

choices.text: Because it requires an Entra ID P2 licence
choices.why: Doing it by hand needs no licence; that is part of why people do it.

prompt: Match each kind of assignment to what it means.
hint: Type and duration are two separate questions.

pairs.right: may activate only between two dates
holds the role between two dates

right_distractors: must be approved for every read

prompt: Which identities does the lesson keep on a permanent active assignment?

choices.text: The platform engineers, since they need Owner every day
choices.why: Those are the people time-bound eligibility is for.

choices.text: Every Global Administrator, as Microsoft requires
choices.why: Microsoft requires no such thing; Global Administrator is a prime candidate for PIM.

choices.text: Readers on testing subscriptions
choices.why: Those need no PIM at all; it is not about permanence.

choices.text: Identities that cannot ask
choices.why: Right. The emergency accounts, and workload identities with no person to answer a prompt.

prompt: A Global Administrator switches on *Access management for Azure resources* to fix a subscription nobody can manage. What does that person now hold, and what should follow?

choices.text: Owner of that one subscription, which stays as a standing role
choices.why: It is not limited to one subscription, and it should not stay.

choices.text: Reader on every subscription, which is harmless and can stay
choices.why: It grants the power to give any role, which is far from Reader.

choices.text: Power to grant any role at `/`; disable it after use
choices.why: Right. User Access Administrator at the root: every subscription in the tenant, so a door to close again.

choices.text: Nothing in Azure, since Entra roles never reach Azure resources
choices.why: This one switch is exactly the Entra role reaching into Azure.

prompt: Which of these can PIM make eligible? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Owner on a resource group
choices.why: Right. An Azure resource role.

choices.text: Global Administrator
choices.why: Right. A Microsoft Entra role.

choices.text: Membership of a group
choices.why: Right. Groups are the third kind.

choices.text: A storage account's access key
choices.why: A key is a secret, not a role. PIM cannot make it ask for anything.

prompt: What is the longest an activation may be set to last, in hours, by Microsoft's documentation?
hint: The slider runs from 1 to it.

prompt: Why does Microsoft recommend at least two approvers for a role that needs approval?
hint: What happens if the only approver is away?

choices.text: So a request does not wait on one person's absence
choices.why: Right. Approval should slow an attacker, not stop an incident.

choices.text: Because both must approve every request
choices.why: One approval suffices; two are about availability.

choices.text: Because an approver must hold Owner, and two Owners are required
choices.why: An approver needs no role of their own.

choices.text: Because PIM refuses to save a role setting with a single approver
choices.why: One approver is allowed; two is a recommendation.

prompt: The settings require multifactor authentication on activation. `ana` passed a second factor at sign-in an hour ago, and activates without being asked again. What does the lesson say about that?
hint: Read Microsoft's warning in the section.

choices.text: It is a defect, and PIM should be reported to Microsoft
choices.why: Microsoft documents this behaviour.

choices.text: It means the setting was never switched on
choices.why: The setting can be on and still accept an earlier second factor.

choices.text: It is impossible: the setting forces a prompt every time
choices.why: Microsoft's documentation says the opposite.

choices.text: Documented; to force a fresh proof, use an authentication context
choices.why: Right. Conditional access, lesson 11, can demand it at activation.

prompt: The on-call developers are eligible for `Shop App Restarter` with a justification and no approval. Why no approval?
hint: Weigh what the role can break against the cost of waiting.

choices.text: Custom roles cannot require approval
choices.why: Any role in PIM can have approval; this was a choice.

choices.text: It breaks little, and a restart at night cannot wait
choices.why: Right. Friction is chosen by what the role can break.

choices.text: Developers are trusted more than platform engineers
choices.why: Trust in people is not the criterion; the power of the role is.

choices.text: Approval applies only to roles at subscription scope
choices.why: Settings are per role and per scope, at any scope.

prompt: What does PIM's audit history record for each activation?
hint: The question it lets you answer about last Tuesday.

choices.text: The commands the person ran while the role was active
choices.why: Commands are in Azure's activity log, not in PIM's history.

choices.text: Only the activations that were refused
choices.why: Every step is recorded, granted or not.

choices.text: Who, which role, where, how long and why
choices.why: Right. A name and a ticket instead of "everybody, always".

choices.text: The person's password at the time of the request
choices.why: No password is ever recorded.

prompt: A periodic question to a reviewer, "should these people still be eligible?", is an access ___.
hint: It is how six-month eligibility gets renewed on purpose.

prompt: In the lesson's `main.tf`, what does the `schedule` block set?

choices.text: How long each activation lasts
choices.why: That is the role's maximum activation, a setting of its own.

choices.text: How long the eligibility itself lasts
choices.why: Right. 180 days of being allowed to activate.

choices.text: When the role may be activated each day
choices.why: PIM has no daily window in this resource.

choices.text: How often the approvers are reminded
choices.why: Notifications are part of the role's settings, not of the assignment.

prompt: `terraform validate` refused the file once `end_date_time` was added under `duration_days`. Why?
hint: How many ways may an eligibility end?

choices.text: The date is in the past
choices.why: 2027-04-30 is in the future; the schema does not compare dates with today.

choices.text: Resource Manager refused a date beyond six months
choices.why: Resource Manager was never asked.

choices.text: Two arguments conflict
choices.why: Right. The provider's schema marks them as conflicting.

choices.text: `end_date_time` needs a time zone other than UTC
choices.why: UTC is fine; the problem is the pair.

prompt: Where are the maximum duration, the approvers and the second factor declared, if not in `azurerm_pim_eligible_role_assignment`?
hint: They belong to the role at a scope, not to one person's eligibility.

choices.text: In a role management policy
choices.why: Right. A separate object attached to the role at a scope.

choices.text: In the role definition, beside `actions`
choices.why: A role definition lists operations; it has no activation settings.

choices.text: Nowhere: they can only be set in the portal
choices.why: The provider has a resource for them.

choices.text: In the `data` block that looks up the role
choices.why: The data block only reads the role's id.

prompt: The shop's team proposes making Owner eligible for the on-call developers, with approval, instead of giving them `Shop App Restarter`. What does the lesson's last paragraph say?

choices.text: Owner with approval is safer, since every activation is reviewed
choices.why: During the hours it is active, it is still Owner.

choices.text: Developers may not be made eligible for any built-in role
choices.why: Anybody may be made eligible for any role.

choices.text: The two are equivalent once the approvers are set
choices.why: One can delete production for four hours; the other can restart an app.

choices.text: PIM limits hours; the narrow role limits power, and both matter
choices.why: Right. Eligibility is not a substitute for least privilege.

prompt: Put one activation of an eligible role in order.
hint: The figure in the second section is the timeline.
items: the person is eligible, with no power yet
the person asks, with a second factor and a justification
the role is active for the hours asked
trap: Approval comes after the request, and the role is active only once it is given.

prompt: A colleague says PIM is pointless because "an attacker with the session just activates the role too". Which of the shop's settings answers that best?
hint: Which setting needs a second person?

choices.text: Approval by another engineer
choices.why: Right. The attacker has to get a second person to agree.

choices.text: The justification
choices.why: Anybody can type a sentence.

choices.text: The 180-day eligibility
choices.why: It decides when eligibility ends, not who can activate.

choices.text: The four-hour maximum
choices.why: It shortens the window but the attacker still gets in.

prompt: Which part of this lesson ran in the lab?

choices.text: An activation of Contributor, refused for want of approval
choices.why: No activation ran: PIM needs a real tenant.

choices.text: Checking the eligibility's file against the provider's schema
choices.why: Right. `validate` ran, twice; `plan` stopped at the sign-in.

choices.text: Reading PIM's audit history for the shop
choices.why: There is no tenant, so there is no history.

choices.text: Creating the eligibility with `terraform apply`
choices.why: Nothing was created; `plan` already stopped.
